tours.d: From the booksellers of rue de la Chaussée-d'Antin and rue de Trévise to the galleries and halls of the 9th arrondissement.
In the footsteps of Guaita, Papus and Erik Satie, from the cabarets of Pigalle to the top of Montmartre.
tours.m: On foot · about 1 h 15 · 2.5 km (final climb to the Butte)

tours.t: From the Louvre to the Opéra: the Rose+Croix in town
tours.d: The 1892 mass, the theosophical Palais-Royal and the galleries of Péladan's last Salons, ending with Mallarmé's Tuesdays.
A hospital, a learned society's hall, a Symbolist café, Delacroix's church and the garret of a Pythagorean abbé.

tours.t: Western magi and final resting places
tours.d: Lévi, the Nabis and the Golden Dawn in Montparnasse, by the Invalides and in Auteuil, Lady Caithness's salon, and the graves of Péladan and Papus.
tours.m: Metro · half a day · scattered sites (about 23 km)

o_bailly.nm: Edmond Bailly's bookshop, the Librairie de l'Art indépendant
o_bailly.tx: Edmond Bailly, a composer and publisher, ran a small bookshop and publishing house here that became the meeting place of Symbolists and occultists. Debussy, Satie, Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, Mallarmé, Péladan and Toulouse-Lautrec dropped in during the late afternoon. Churton makes it the gateway to the whole of occult Paris in the Belle Époque.
o_bailly.stn: Commercial building in the department-store district; nothing marks the former bookshop.
o_bailly.w: Churton dates the opening to 1888; other sources give October 1889. The bookshop later moved and did not close until 1917.

o_durand_ruel.nm: Galerie Durand-Ruel – first Salon de la Rose+Croix
o_durand_ruel.tx: On 10 March 1892 the first Salon de la Rose+Croix opened here, organized by Joséphin Péladan and funded by Count Antoine de La Rochefoucauld. The crowds were so large that traffic in the neighborhood came to a standstill. Symbolist and Idealist painters exhibited, with music by Satie in the background.
o_durand_ruel.stn: The Durand-Ruel gallery has left the premises.
o_durand_ruel.w: The Durand-Ruel gallery had two entrances (16, rue Laffitte and 11, rue Le Peletier); the marker is placed on the rue Le Peletier side, at estimated coordinates.

o_trevise.nm: Chamuel's Librairie du Merveilleux and offices of L'Initiation
o_trevise.tx: On Papus's advice, Lucien Mauchel, known as Chamuel, opened the Librairie du Merveilleux here. The address became the nerve center of Papus's occultism: the journal L'Initiation, the Martinist Order, the Independent Group for Esoteric Studies, and meetings of Jules Doinel's Gnostic Church. Papus received the curious and the initiated here every week.
o_trevise.stn: Commercial premises; Churton publishes a recent photograph.

o_bodiniere.nm: Théâtre de la Bodinière – the Rites of Isis
o_bodiniere.tx: In this small lecture and performance hall, Samuel MacGregor Mathers and his wife Moina presented their “Rites of Isis” to the public in March 1899, a theatrical reconstruction of an Egyptian cult that had begun in their temple in Auteuil. The show intrigued the press and drew curious members of fashionable Paris.
o_bodiniere.stn: The hall closed in 1902; the address is now a restaurant.
o_bodiniere.w: Churton places the Bodinière on the hill of Montmartre; it was in fact on rue Saint-Lazare, in the 9th arrondissement. Coordinates estimated from the street number.

o_moreau.tx: From 1895 the painter Gustave Moreau, a guiding figure for the Symbolists, turned his house and studio into a museum of his work while living in the first-floor apartment. He visited the first Salon de la Rose+Croix without exhibiting there. Churton presents the place as a sanctuary for lovers of Symbolist art.
o_moreau.ch: 10. The Salon of the Century (and plate 11)

o_guaita_pigalle.nm: Stanislas de Guaita's first apartment (shared with Péladan)
o_guaita_pigalle.tx: After the Latin Quarter, the young Stanislas de Guaita moved to rue Pigalle and invited his new friend Joséphin Péladan to share the apartment. The arrangement did not last, as the two personalities clashed. This was still the address Guaita gave Oswald Wirth when they first met.
o_guaita_pigalle.w: The street numbering may have changed since the 1880s; coordinates estimated.
o_guaita_pigalle.oq: Premier appartement de Stanislas de Guaita Paris

o_chat_noir.ad: 12, rue Victor-Massé (alors rue de Laval), 75009 Paris
o_chat_noir.tx: Founded in 1881 on boulevard de Rochechouart by Rodolphe Salis, the Chat Noir moved here in 1885. At the end of 1887, Erik Satie introduced himself there as a “gymnopédiste” and was taken on as a pianist. With its shadow theater and its magazine, the cabaret often crossed paths with the world of Symbolists and occultists.
o_chat_noir.stn: Private building; the cabaret closed in 1897.
o_chat_noir.w: The first Chat Noir (1881-1885) was at 84, boulevard de Rochechouart; the sign on boulevard de Clichy is a 20th-century revival.

o_condorcet.tx: Churton presents this building as Erik Satie's first proper home in Paris, occupied around 1888, at the time of the Gymnopédies and the Sarabandes, until the money ran out. The composer was then frequenting the Chat Noir and Bailly's bookshop, where he met Debussy.
o_condorcet.w: Address known only from the caption of a plate in the book; exact dates not verified. Coordinates estimated.

o_rollin.tx: Gérard Encausse, the future Papus, studied at this school, which moved to avenue Trudaine in 1876. Several of his classmates, including Lucien Mauchel (Chamuel), later formed a small Sunday literary circle around him, the core of his future publishing and initiatic ventures.
o_rollin.stn: Collège-lycée Jacques-Decour, to be seen from outside.

o_guaita_trudaine.tx: In January 1887 Guaita moved into the ground floor of this building and assembled a large occult library there. On Thursday evenings he received Papus, Péladan, Abbé Roca, Lady Caithness, Michelet, Barrès and Saint-Yves d'Alveydre around the tea table. Legend had it that the apartment was haunted.
o_guaita_trudaine.w: Churton writes once that Guaita died in 1898 (ch. 5), but elsewhere gives the exact date of 19 December 1897 (ch. 14), which is the correct one; he died at the Château d'Alteville. Coordinates estimated from the street number.
o_guaita_trudaine.oq: Appartement de Stanislas de Guaita Paris

o_clou.tx: A cabaret-restaurant with a shadow theater run by Miguel Utrillo, the Auberge du Clou brought together Catalan painters and friends of Satie. Here the composer worked on Uspud, a “Christian ballet” written with Contamine de Latour, and through this circle he met Suzanne Valadon. Debussy also frequented the place.
o_clou.stn: A restaurant still occupies the address (Le Clou).
o_clou.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number.

o_cortot.tx: Satie lived in a small room at the top of the Butte from 1890 to 1898, “above his creditors” as he put it. There he composed the Gnossiennes, lived out his 1893 affair with Suzanne Valadon, and that same year founded his Metropolitan Church of Art of Jesus the Conductor, of which he was the only member.
o_cortot.stn: Commemorative plaque on the facade; the Musée de Montmartre is next door (12, rue Cortot).

o_auxerrois.tx: On the morning of 10 March 1892, Péladan had a solemn Mass of the Holy Spirit celebrated here to open the first Salon de la Rose+Croix. Excerpts from Wagner's Parsifal were played, preceded by fanfares for harps and trumpets by Erik Satie. The guests then drove to the Durand-Ruel gallery.

o_vefour.acc: Palais Royal – Musée du Louvre (1, 7) / Pyramides (7, 14)
o_vefour.tx: In a private room of this famous café-restaurant at the Palais-Royal, the theosophical journal Le Lotus held an evening at which Papus spoke in public for the first time. Michelet, who had helped organize it, judged him a very poor speaker at the time; Papus improved quickly.
o_vefour.w: Churton places the evening at 8, rue de Montpensier; the Grand Véfour's address is 17, rue de Beaujolais, under the arcades of the Palais-Royal. Exact date not given in the book.

o_arts_reunis.nm: Galerie des Arts réunis – 1896 Salon de la Rose+Croix
o_arts_reunis.tx: The fifth Salon de la Rose+Croix was held in March 1896 in this vast, electrically lit gallery. With Péladan away on his honeymoon, Léonce de Larmandie organized the exhibition. More than eight thousand visitors came on the first day; the poster, showing a hero brandishing the severed head of Zola, caused a scandal.
o_arts_reunis.w: Churton writes “28 rue de l'Opéra”; this is most likely avenue de l'Opéra. Number and coordinates not verified.

o_petit.nm: Galerie Georges Petit – last Salon de la Rose+Croix
o_petit.tx: The dealer Georges Petit hosted the sixth and final Salon de la Rose+Croix, from 5 to 21 March 1897. Fifteen thousand people crowded in on opening day. Péladan, then in Belgium, left the organization to Larmandie; 217 works were hung, notably by Séon and Osbert.
o_petit.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number.

o_mallarme.tx: Every Tuesday evening, Mallarmé received poets, painters and musicians in his small apartment. Churton mentions these “Tuesdays” among the Symbolist gatherings attended by Gauguin, Charles Morice and regulars of Bailly's bookshop, which published a musical setting of a poem by Mallarmé.
o_mallarme.w: The book mentions the Tuesdays without giving the address, which is known from other sources. Coordinates estimated.

o_charite.ad: Angle du boulevard Saint-Germain et de la rue des Saints-Pères (45, rue des Saints-Pères), 75006 Paris
o_charite.tx: As a medical student, Papus attended the teaching of Dr. Jules Luys here, a specialist in hypnosis whose interest in magnetism he shared. Churton relates that he brought Anatole France here in an attempt to interest him in occultism. Papus would die in this hospital in 1916.
o_charite.stn: Hospital demolished in the 1930s; the site is occupied by the Saints-Pères medical faculty.
o_charite.w: Papus's death at the Charité comes from standard biographies, not from Churton's book. Coordinates placed at the corner of the two streets.
o_charite.oq: Ancien hôpital de la Charité Paris

o_geographie.nm: Société de géographie – Léo Taxil's confession
o_geographie.tx: On 19 April 1897, a crowd of Catholics, Freemasons and journalists waited here for the appearance of Diana Vaughan, supposedly a repentant member of a Luciferian sect. Instead Léo Taxil took the stage to reveal that the whole affair, his books and his revelations had been a hoax kept up for twelve years.
o_geographie.stn: Headquarters of the Société de géographie, to be seen from outside.
o_geographie.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number.

o_peladan_seine.nm: Lodgings of Péladan and Henriette Maillat
o_peladan_seine.ad: Angle de la rue de Seine et de la rue des Beaux-Arts, 75006 Paris
o_peladan_seine.tx: For a time Péladan lived with Henriette Maillat on the top floor of a house on the corner of these two streets. This woman, who later had a brief affair with Huysmans, inspired some features of Mme Chantelouve in his Là-bas (1891). The neighborhood was one of publishers and art schools.
o_peladan_seine.w: The book gives neither the number nor the exact dates; marker placed at the intersection.
o_peladan_seine.oq: Logement de Péladan et Henriette Maillat Paris

o_sulpice.nm: Church of Saint-Sulpice – Chapel of the Holy Angels (Delacroix)
o_sulpice.tx: Delacroix's murals in the Chapel of the Holy Angels, completed in 1861, fascinated Maurice Barrès. In his writings for the Catholic Rose+Croix, Péladan counted Delacroix among his “saints” and cited these angels as a source of daily inspiration. Éliphas Lévi had been a seminarian at Saint-Sulpice.
o_sulpice.stn: Church; the chapel is on the right as you enter.

o_voltaire.tx: This café near the Odéon theater was a meeting place for the Symbolists: Verlaine, Moréas, Mallarmé, Gauguin, Charles Morice, Aurier and Redon debated there. Churton brings Gauguin here before his departure for Tahiti, and it was in a café in this neighborhood that Barrès introduced Michelet to Guaita.
o_voltaire.stn: Café closed in the mid-20th century; premises of the publisher Flammarion since 1956, with a Histoire de Paris information panel.
o_voltaire.w: The book does not say that the Michelet-Guaita meeting took place specifically at the Café Voltaire, only “near the Odéon”.
o_voltaire.ch: 10. The Salon of the Century (and ch. 5)

o_lacuria.tx: Abbé Paul-François-Gaspard Lacuria, author of Les Harmonies de l'être, lived poor and almost blind in a garret filled with books and scores. Young seekers of mysticism nicknamed him the “French Pythagoras”. Péladan, who revered him, recounted climbing up to see him one cold afternoon.
o_lacuria.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number.

o_levi.tx: On 3 December 1861, the Englishman Kenneth Mackenzie, a future member of the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, visited Éliphas Lévi in his apartment. Lévi showed him a prophecy attributed to Paracelsus foretelling the return of the occult sciences. The account appeared in 1873 in an English Rosicrucian journal.
o_levi.w: The numbering of avenue du Maine may have changed since 1861; location to be confirmed. Lévi died in 1875 and was buried in Ivry, outside Paris.

o_ranson.tx: Every Saturday, Maurice Denis, Paul Sérusier and other Nabis met in Paul Ranson's studio, which they called the “Temple”. Their discussions gave rise to the manifesto Denis published in 1890. Steeped in theosophy and Symbolism, the group adopted names and rituals like a brotherhood.
o_ranson.w: The street number comes from a museum source (Yvelines department), not from the book. Coordinates estimated.
o_ranson.ch: 10. The Salon of the Century (and plate 9)

o_duquesne.nm: The Mathers' apartment – first Ahathoor temple
o_duquesne.tx: After settling in Paris, Samuel MacGregor Mathers and Moina Mathers lived briefly on rue de Miromesnil, then in this apartment near the Invalides. This is where the Golden Dawn's Ahathoor Temple No. 7 first met; it was consecrated on 6 January 1894 in the presence of Annie Horniman and William Wynn Westcott.
o_duquesne.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number. Historic site: no temple exists here today.

o_mozart.nm: The Mathers' villa in Auteuil – Ahathoor temple
o_mozart.tx: From 1895 the Mathers lived in a villa with three entrances (87, avenue Mozart; 43, rue Ribera; 41, rue de la Source), with a garden, a temple room decorated with Egyptian deities and private living quarters. Papus was received as a neophyte here on 23 March 1895. Crowley came here for the first time in January 1900.
o_mozart.w: Coordinates estimated; the villa may have been demolished or altered. Historic site: no temple exists here today.
o_mozart.oq: Villa des Mathers à Auteuil Paris

o_holyrood.nm: Lady Caithness's “Holyrood” mansion, Duchess of Pomar
o_holyrood.tx: A wealthy theosophist widow, Marie de Pomar, Countess of Caithness, received occult Paris every Wednesday, from spring to autumn, in her town house, part of which imitates the Scottish palace of Holyrood. Spiritualist séances dedicated to Mary Stuart were held here, and Jules Doinel had his Gnostic Church consecrated here in 1890.
o_holyrood.stn: Mansion demolished, replaced by a modern building.
o_holyrood.w: Coordinates estimated from the street number. Churton, following Doinel's account preserved by Déodat Roché, places the founding séance at Lady Caithness's in the autumn of 1889 and the formation of the Church in 1890; these details rest solely on the testimony of Doinel and those close to him.
o_holyrood.oq: Hôtel « Holyrood » de Lady Caithness Paris

o_peladan_tombe.acc: Porte de Clichy (13, RER C) / Brochant (13)
o_peladan_tombe.nm: Grave of Joséphin Péladan, Cimetière des Batignolles
o_peladan_tombe.ad: Cimetière des Batignolles, 8, rue Saint-Just, 75017 Paris (6e division)
o_peladan_tombe.tx: Joséphin Péladan, the “Sâr”, died in June 1918 in Neuilly-sur-Seine, of food poisoning according to Churton. He is buried in the Cimetière des Batignolles. Founder of the Order of the Catholic Rose+Croix and organizer of the Salons from 1892 to 1897, he left behind a considerable body of novels.
o_peladan_tombe.w: Division given by the cemetery's list of burials; exact location of the grave not verified, marker placed at the center of the cemetery.

o_papus_tombe.ad: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise, 16, rue du Repos, 75020 Paris (93e division)
o_papus_tombe.tx: Gérard Encausse, known as Papus, physician, prolific author and Grand Master of the Martinist Order, died on 25 October 1916 at the age of 51. His grave, in the 93rd division of Père-Lachaise, lists his titles and bears a thought on prayer; his son, Dr. Philippe Encausse, is also buried there.

h: Rue de la Chaussée-d'Antin, long lined with aristocratic mansions, gradually turned commercial under the Third Republic. At number 11, in premises that had housed Édouard Dujardin's La Revue indépendante, Edmond Bailly (1850-1916) opened the Librairie de l'Art indépendant. It was at once a shop, a publishing house and an informal salon, a few hundred meters from the Opéra and the grands boulevards, in a neighborhood then undergoing rapid change.

According to Churton, who draws on the memoirs of Victor-Émile Michelet, the place attracted more artists than occultists in the strict sense. Debussy is said to have met Satie there; one could run into Mallarmé, Villiers, Henri de Régnier, Odilon Redon or Péladan. Bailly published Symbolist poets, scores and esoteric texts, including a translation of the Tao Te Ching by Matgioi in 1893. According to Michelet, the atmosphere was less “charged with occult effluvia” than at Chamuel's on rue de Trévise.

The shop later moved and Bailly ended his days in relative obscurity; the publishing house disappeared in 1917, shortly after his death. Today number 11 lies at the heart of the department-store shopping district, and no visible trace recalls the bookshop. Churton publishes a recent photograph of the facade. The site remains above all a symbolic landmark: the place where music, poetry and esotericism met at the end of the 1880s.

Paul Durand-Ruel, the Impressionists' historic dealer, owned a gallery that opened onto both rue Laffitte and rue Le Peletier, in the heart of the 9th arrondissement's art-dealing district. Nothing predisposed him to host painters hostile to Naturalism and Impressionism. Churton stresses that it was the charm and above all the money of Count Antoine de La Rochefoucauld, Péladan's patron, that made it possible to rent his rooms in 1892.

The first Salon de la Rose+Croix opened on Thursday 10 March 1892, after a mass at Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois. According to the figures quoted by Churton, hundreds of carriages were parked and the police had to stop the traffic. Visitors in the first hours paid a high price. On show were Aman-Jean, Bernard, Delville, Filiger, Hodler, Khnopff, Osbert, Séon, Schwabe and many others, in rooms decorated with flowers; Puvis de Chavannes, Moreau, Verlaine and even Zola came by.

This society success would not last: the gallery, deemed too expensive, was no longer rented for the following Salons, and the break with La Rochefoucauld came as early as the spring of 1892: Péladan, furious at being stripped of the direction of the musical evenings, declared him “anathema” and expelled him from the Order. The Durand-Ruel gallery has since left rue Le Peletier. The address remains a milestone in the history of Symbolist art: it was here that Péladan's aesthetic Rose+Croix first showed itself to the wider Parisian public. For the passer-by, it is just a shopfront on a commercial street, but the neighbourhood still bears traces of the old Parisian art market.

Rue de Trévise is a quiet street in the 9th arrondissement, about a kilometer east of the Chaussée-d'Antin. Around 1888, Gérard Encausse, known as Papus, encouraged a former classmate from the Collège Rollin, Lucien Mauchel, to open a specialist bookshop there. Mauchel took the pseudonym Chamuel, the name of an archangel in the Kabbalistic tradition, and called his shop the Librairie du Merveilleux. Churton opens his chapter on Papus by imagining Péladan arriving by cab in front of number 29.

For about ten years the shop served as office and meeting room for almost all of Papus's ventures: the journal L'Initiation, the Martinist Order, the Independent Group for Esoteric Studies and its courses. In 1892 Jules Doinel held the first synod of his Gnostic Church there, with the journal's team. Michelet found the place more “charged with occult effluvia” than Bailly's bookshop, but less frequented by artists.

After the death of Lady Caithness in November 1895, rue de Trévise on the contrary became, according to Churton, the main hub of occult Paris, even though internal quarrels made the movement less and less unified; Chamuel continued his publishing business. Today the ground floor of no. 29 is an ordinary shop, with no plaque or sign recalling this history. Yet it is one of the most important addresses of late nineteenth-century French occultism. The street itself has kept its nineteenth-century buildings and its calm, which helps one imagine the comings and goings of the readers of L'Initiation.

La Bodinière, opened in 1890 by Charles Bodinier, was a small multipurpose hall on rue Saint-Lazare: lectures, exhibitions, shadow theater, recitals and avant-garde shows followed one another there. It belonged to the network of intermediate venues, somewhere between cabaret and theater, typical of Belle Époque Paris, where a cultivated public came in search of novelty. It closed in 1902. Its eclectic program made it a convenient place to present shows that had no place in the major theaters.

Churton explains that the Mathers, once settled in Paris, launched a semi-public revival of the cult of Isis, with Moina playing the high priestess and Samuel the high priest. Begun in their house in Passy-Auteuil, these ceremonies were brought to the stage of the Bodinière in March 1899. Questioned by an English journalist, Mathers presented the venture as a remedy for the decadence of the age rather than as one more provocation. The audience discovered costumes, invocations and dances inspired by ancient Egypt, in a production designed by the Mathers themselves.

The episode marks the meeting of the British Golden Dawn and Parisian society life, at a time when the order was going through a serious crisis in England. Aleister Crowley, who frequented the Mathers from 1900, is an indirect witness. Nothing at 18, rue Saint-Lazare suggests a theater anymore: a restaurant now occupies the premises. One has to look at the facade and remember that a reconstructed Egyptian cult was performed here before Parisian spectators on the eve of 1900.

Gustave Moreau (1826-1898) lived with his parents in this town house in the Nouvelle-Athènes, an artists' quarter of the 9th arrondissement. His paintings of Salome, Orpheus or Oedipus, saturated with jewels, myths and symbols, fascinated the Decadent writers, starting with Huysmans in À rebours. A professor at the École des beaux-arts, he also trained a generation of painters, from Rouault to Matisse. His house on rue de La Rochefoucauld, bought by his parents in 1852, was his home and workplace for nearly half a century.

Churton counts him among the figures that occultists and Symbolists regarded as masters. Péladan admired him and wanted him to exhibit at the Rose+Croix; Moreau declined, but came to see the 1892 Salon at Durand-Ruel's. Shortly before his death he decided to bequeath his house and thousands of works to the State, and had the building enlarged to turn it into a museum while continuing to live on the first floor.

The museum opened in 1903. It preserves the two-level studio, the spiral staircase and the painter's private apartment, and remains one of the few places of Symbolist Paris that can be visited as it was. It is a natural stop for anyone wanting to see the visual imagination admired by Péladan's circle. The visit also lets you see numerous drawings and sketches stored in cabinets with hinged panels, designed by the painter to display his work.

Rue Pigalle, renamed rue Jean-Baptiste-Pigalle, climbs from the Trinité toward place Pigalle, at the foot of Montmartre. In the 1880s it was a neighborhood of painters, models and literary cafés, a short walk from the Nouvelle-Athènes. Stanislas de Guaita (1861-1897), a wealthy poet from Lorraine who had come to study in Paris, left the Latin Quarter to settle here, drawn by the artistic life of the Right Bank. The young man arrived with a solid family fortune, a passion for poetry and a growing interest in Kabbalah and magic.

Churton reports, following Michelet, that Guaita invited Péladan to share his lodgings, but that the future “Sâr”'s difficult temper soon wore out the friendship. The two men, of opposite temperaments, parted ways; yet in 1888 they would together found the Kabbalistic Order of the Rose-Croix. It was also from 24, rue Pigalle that Guaita wrote to Oswald Wirth, his future secretary and tarot designer, to invite him to dinner. Wirth went on to become one of Guaita's most loyal collaborators, entrusted with producing symbolic drawings.

Guaita then moved a few hundred meters east, to avenue Trudaine. The building on rue Pigalle is now an ordinary residence, with no plaque. The site illustrates how geographically close these circles were: most of the players in Parisian occultism lived within a few minutes' walk of one another, between Pigalle, Trudaine and the Chaussée-d'Antin. This proximity encouraged the visits, quarrels and reconciliations that fill Churton's book.

src.t: Occult Paris (Churton, 2016), ch. 5, p. 131; ch. 7, p. 191

h: The Chat Noir is the most famous artistic cabaret of Montmartre. Rodolphe Salis opened it in 1881 at 84, boulevard de Rochechouart, then moved it in 1885 to a town house on rue de Laval, now rue Victor-Massé. Poems were read and songs sung there, and its shadow theater, run notably by Henri Rivière and Charles de Sivry, drew a very mixed public. The cabaret also published an illustrated paper bearing its name, which brought together the cartoonists, poets and songwriters of Montmartre.

Churton places here Erik Satie's arrival in artistic Paris: in December 1887, accompanied by the poet Contamine de Latour, the young Norman introduced himself to Salis as a “gymnopédiste” and became the cabaret's pianist. He is said to have worked on his Gymnopédies here. Péladan also frequented the establishment, although Salis had little liking for him and the cabaret's journal echoed this. In early 1893, at the height of the Boullan affair, Churton imagines the cabaret regulars joking about the “fluids” used in bewitchment, without singling out the Chat Noir in particular. The room thus served as a link between Montmartre bohemia and the more serious circles of the Chaussée-d'Antin.

The Chat Noir closed in 1897, shortly after Salis's death; other cabarets later took over the building. The building on rue Victor-Massé, a stone's throw from place Pigalle, is now private. Steinlen's cat, which has become a tourist image, mostly recalls the sign, but the 1885 address is the one Satie and the Symbolists knew. Visitors can combine this stop with nearby place Pigalle, where several cafés frequented by the same artists once stood.

Rue Condorcet links rue de Maubeuge to rue des Martyrs, south of Montmartre, in a neighborhood of modest housing and workshops. At the end of the 1880s many penniless artists settled here, halfway between the cabarets of Pigalle and the shops of the Chaussée-d'Antin. Erik Satie, who had arrived from Honfleur and fallen out with his father, was then trying to make a living from his music. The young musician was in his early twenties and lived on odd jobs as a pianist.

In the plate section of his book, Churton publishes a photograph of 50, rue Condorcet, described as Satie's first decent lodging, occupied around 1888 until his finances collapsed. This was when he composed the Gymnopédies and the Sarabandes, played at the Chat Noir and became friends with Debussy at Bailly's. The book gives no further details about this stay. The photograph shows the facade of an apartment building typical of the neighborhood.

For lack of money, Satie then moved up to the top of the Butte, on rue Cortot. The building on rue Condorcet is now a private residence, with no known plaque. It can serve as a stop between Pigalle and avenue Trudaine for following the composer's early years in Paris. It shows how the stages of Satie's life followed one another only a few hundred meters apart, from rue Condorcet to the Chat Noir and then rue Cortot. From here the walker can reach avenue Trudaine in two minutes.

The Collège Rollin, successor to the old Collège Sainte-Barbe, left the Latin Quarter in 1876 for large new buildings on avenue Trudaine, at the foot of Montmartre. It became the Lycée Rollin in 1919 and, since the Liberation, has borne the name of Jacques Decour, a teacher and Resistance fighter shot in 1942. The school faces the square d'Anvers. The move accompanied the rapid urbanization of southern Montmartre, and the school took in the sons of the local bourgeoisie. Papus completed part of his secondary education here before studying medicine.

Churton recalls that Papus was a pupil here. Later, living modestly near the Gare de l'Est, he gathered five or six former Rollin classmates on Sunday mornings to talk literature and philosophy: Georges Polti, Émile Gary and above all Lucien Mauchel, the future bookseller Chamuel. Michelet ironically compared this group to a Pythagorean school. These school friendships gave rise to the Librairie du Merveilleux and the journal L'Initiation. Papus remained close to these companions all his life.

The building, still occupied by a public secondary school, can be seen from avenue Trudaine. Together with number 20 on the same avenue, where Guaita lived, and the Auberge du Clou a little further on, it forms a small area where several of the book's addresses are concentrated. It makes a good starting point for a short walk through this neighborhood, where the great figures of Parisian occultism lived, studied or met between 1880 and 1900. The nearby square d'Anvers offers a place to rest.

Avenue Trudaine, a broad tree-lined street in southern Montmartre, is lined with 19th-century bourgeois apartment buildings. In January 1887 Stanislas de Guaita rented a ground-floor apartment at number 20. From then on he spent most of the year there, except for summers at the family château of Alteville in Lorraine, and assembled a remarkable library of works on Kabbalah, alchemy and magic. The apartment looks onto the avenue, a few steps from the Collège Rollin and the Auberge du Clou.

According to Churton, Guaita held Thursday evening gatherings there where people crowded “like alchemists around the athanor”: Papus, Péladan, Abbé Roca, Lady Caithness, Michelet, Barrès, Saint-Yves d'Alveydre. This was the heart of the Kabbalistic Order of the Rose-Croix, founded in 1888. It was also from here, according to his opponents, that the so-called magical war against Abbé Boullan was launched, which Huysmans and Jules Bois denounced in 1893. These sessions mixed learned conversation, readings and plans for initiatic orders.

Guaita, increasingly reclusive and dependent on drugs, died at 36. The apartment's reputation as a haunted place, reported by Churton, belongs to legend. The building is now private and can be seen from the avenue; Churton publishes a recent photograph of it. His books on Satanism and black magic, collected under the title Le Serpent de la Genèse, remained unfinished. His library, dispersed after his death, fed the market for esoteric books for decades. No plaque recalls his time here.

The Auberge du Clou opened at the end of the 1880s on the corner of avenue Trudaine, in a neighborhood full of cabarets. In the basement, a shadow theater in the spirit of the Chat Noir was run by the Catalan painter and critic Miguel Utrillo, around whom gravitated several Spanish artists living in Montmartre, such as Santiago Rusiñol and Ramon Casas. The establishment combined a restaurant on the ground floor with small stages, a formula then very much in vogue at the foot of the Butte.

Churton relates that Satie, very short of money after the 1892 Salon de la Rose+Croix, had his ballet Uspud, to a libretto by Contamine de Latour, performed or presented here. Stung by the regulars' criticism, he bet that he would get it accepted by the Opéra, which failed. It was in this circle that he met Suzanne Valadon, a former acrobat and model and the mother of young Maurice Utrillo; their affair began in January 1893.

In musical memory the place is also associated with the first meetings between Satie and Debussy, even though Churton places those at Bailly's. The address still houses a restaurant, making it one of the few places on the route where you can still sit down. The decor has changed, but the location on the corner of avenue Trudaine remains the same, a few meters from Guaita's former home. In a few steps you can thus link the Catalan artists' cabaret and the Lorraine magus's salon.

Rue Cortot is a peaceful street at the top of Montmartre, a few steps from the vineyards and from the house that is now home to the Musée de Montmartre. In 1890 this was still a semi-rural village, without the completed Sacré-Cœur basilica. Erik Satie rented a tiny room here, where he lived in poverty until he left for Arcueil in 1898. The street is named after an early 19th-century sculptor, and several painters, including Renoir, had studios here.

Churton places the composition of the Gnossiennes here, a title he links to gnosis. In January 1893 Suzanne Valadon moved in with Satie for a six-month affair, the composer's only known romantic relationship. After the breakup, Satie created, on paper, the Metropolitan Church of Art of Jesus the Conductor, of which he proclaimed himself “parcier” and chapel master. Churton sees it as a personal and defensive version of Péladan's Rose+Croix.

A plaque now recalls that the composer lived in this house from 1890 to 1898. The building is private, but the street is open to all, and the neighboring museum evokes the artistic life of the Butte in the same period. Satie left for Arcueil in October 1898, after several years of great poverty. You can extend the visit toward place du Tertre or rue de l'Abreuvoir, bearing in mind that the neighborhood was then much more rural.

Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, opposite the Louvre colonnade, was long the parish church of the kings living in the palace. Its Flamboyant Gothic porch and its bell tower are associated in collective memory with the signal for the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572. In the 19th century the church was restored and remained a prestigious parish at the heart of the Right Bank. It faced the Louvre, then still shared between museum and government offices, and remained an aristocratic parish.

Péladan wanted his Salon to be a Catholic undertaking as much as an aesthetic one. He therefore arranged for a Mass of the Holy Spirit to precede the opening on 10 March 1892. According to the program quoted by Churton, passages from Parsifal were heard, including the prelude and the Good Friday Spell, after three fanfares of the Order composed by Satie. The ceremony gave the Salon a liturgical flavor and helped make it a sensation in the press. Satie was then the order's official composer.

The church is still open for worship and visits. Nothing there recalls the Rose+Croix, but the place lets you imagine the procession of carriages that then headed north to rue Le Peletier, a kilometer away. It is also a convenient starting point for a walk toward the Opéra. Allow about fifteen minutes on foot to follow the same route as the guests, via rue du Louvre or rue de Richelieu.

Since the end of the 18th century, Le Grand Véfour has occupied part of the galleries of the Palais-Royal. First a café, then a luxury restaurant, it has seen politicians, writers and artists come through, from Bonaparte to Victor Hugo. Its neoclassical decor, with its painted canvases under glass, has been preserved and listed as a historic monument. In the 1880s it remained a prestigious venue where private rooms could be hired for dinners, banquets or evenings organized by journals.

Churton relates that at the time when Papus attended Félix-Krishna Gaboriau's Isis theosophical lodge, before founding his own Hermès lodge, the journal Le Lotus organized an evening in a room at the Véfour. Victor-Émile Michelet, who had helped organize it, was disappointed by Gérard Encausse's first attempt at public speaking, which he found hesitant. Some time later, however, he observed that Papus knew how to hold an audience, at the cost of a certain simplification. He would become a very active lecturer.

The restaurant is still in business and its facade can be seen from the garden and the arcades of the Palais-Royal. The place is a reminder that Parisian theosophy in the 1880s also met in fashionable settings, far from the back rooms of bookshops. The gardens and neighboring galleries are open to all, and you can walk along the arcades to rue de Beaujolais. At the time the palace still housed many cafés, restaurants and clubs.

h: Avenue de l'Opéra, laid out under the Second Empire and completed in 1878, was in the 1890s one of the most prominent shopping streets in Paris. Private galleries rented their rooms to artists' societies. The Galerie des Arts réunis had a space large enough to hold thousands of visitors, and electric daytime lighting that was still rare at the time. It stood halfway between the Louvre and the Opéra.

After the 1894 and 1895 Salons in a small gallery on rue de la Paix, Péladan looked for somewhere larger: his marriage in January 1896 to a niece of Larmandie had earned him enormous publicity. The March 1896 Salon was organized by Larmandie while Péladan was in Venice. Churton reports more than eight thousand visitors on opening day and describes the controversy over the poster by Armand Point and Léonard Sarluys, in which Zola's head can be recognized.

The gallery disappeared long ago. All that remains is the memory of a popular exhibition, proof that Rosicrucian aesthetics attracted a wide public in the mid-1890s, despite the mockery of the critics. The address can be found at the number given, but nothing now distinguishes it from the other buildings on the avenue. Yet the 1896 Salon was one of the best attended of the series, and its famous poster is now held in several public collections. It illustrates the bitterness of the debate between Idealists and Naturalists at the end of the century.

Georges Petit (1856-1920) was, along with Durand-Ruel, one of the great Parisian art dealers of the late 19th century. His gallery on rue de Sèze, near the Madeleine, was renowned for its vast, luxurious rooms; major international exhibitions were held there, including retrospectives of Monet and Rodin. After Petit's death the business passed to Bernheim-Jeune and the gallery closed in 1933. It attracted a wealthy, cosmopolitan clientele.

According to Churton, it was Petit himself who offered his rooms to the Order of the Catholic Rose+Croix for the 1897 Salon. The exhibition ran from 5 to 21 March and drew a considerable crowd from the opening. The catalogue asserted that man needs mystery, not to penetrate it but to experience it. Armand Point withdrew with a flourish, and Péladan, who was absent, left Larmandie to hang the works. Alexandre Séon, a friend of Péladan, was given particular prominence.

This Salon marked the end of the adventure: Péladan never organized another. The address is a reminder that the aesthetic Rose+Croix, which began in an Impressionist gallery, ended in one of the most fashionable galleries in Paris. The gallery itself has disappeared, and the building retains no visible trace of the exhibition. The Madeleine area, however, remains a district of luxury shops and dealers, as it was at the end of the 19th century. After 1897 the Rose+Croix artists pursued their careers separately, and several of them joined other exhibiting societies.

Stéphane Mallarmé, an English teacher at a lycée, moved in 1875 into a modest apartment on rue de Rome, near the Gare Saint-Lazare. From the early 1880s he received an ever wider circle of writers and artists there every Tuesday. These gatherings, known as the “Tuesdays”, became one of the centers of the Symbolist movement. The small, plain apartment was nothing like a fashionable salon. The poet would speak standing by the stove, before an attentive audience.

Churton mentions these evenings in connection with Gauguin and Charles Morice, who attended them around 1891, and among the habits of the Nabis and the Symbolist critics. Mallarmé was close to several regulars of the Art indépendant; Edmond Bailly in fact published a musical setting of his poem “Apparition”. Without being an occultist, the poet shared the idea of a language charged with mystery, which fascinated esoteric circles. He was also in contact with Villiers de L'Isle-Adam and several authors published by Bailly.

Mallarmé died in 1898 at Valvins. The building on rue de Rome is now a private residence, to be viewed from the pavement. The address, a little apart from the other places on the route, usefully completes the map of Symbolist Paris, where poetry, painting and esotericism met. It is worth remembering that for nearly twenty years the Tuesdays brought together successive generations of writers, from André Gide to Paul Valéry. A brief visit is enough.

h: The Hôpital de la Charité, founded in the 17th century by the Brothers of Saint John of God, stretched along rue des Saints-Pères, at the corner of the future boulevard Saint-Germain. A renowned teaching hospital, it was home to great clinicians. It was demolished in the 1930s and replaced by the buildings of the Saints-Pères medical faculty. Medical students attended lessons and ward rounds there, and several departments took an interest in nervous diseases. Research on hypnosis and suggestion then drew many curious onlookers.

Churton reports that Papus, then a non-resident student in the department of Dr. Jules Luys, an ardent explorer of hypnosis and suggestion, once took the writer Anatole France to watch some experiments. He hoped to draw him toward occultism; Michelet thought this hope futile, France remaining in his eyes a brilliant dilettante. In 1891 Luys, along with Flammarion and others, signed an honorary diploma presented to Papus. Papus, who defended his medical thesis in 1894, was thus keen to give his research scientific credibility.

Papus, called up as a doctor during the First World War, died of tuberculosis at the Charité on 25 October 1916, according to his biographers. The present building, in a 1930s-1950s style, retains nothing of the old hospital. The corner of the two streets remains a landmark for recalling the link between medicine, hypnosis and occultism at the end of the 19th century. Today visitors pass a university facade. No plaque recalls the old hospital or Papus's time there.

The Société de géographie, founded in 1821, moved in 1878 into a mansion on boulevard Saint-Germain with a large lecture hall. Explorers reported on their expeditions there. Like other learned societies' halls, it was also rented out for public lectures, which explains how one of the most famous hoaxes of the end of the century came to be staged there. The building is a few steps from the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in a neighborhood of publishers and learned institutions.

Léo Taxil, a former anticlerical who had apparently converted, had been publishing revelations since 1885 about a supposed satanic cult, Palladism, said to control Freemasonry. His main character, Diana Vaughan, was finally to appear on 19 April 1897. Before a packed hall, Taxil explained that he had made it all up. Churton discusses the affair because Palladism was set against Gnostic and Martinist circles, and because Éliphas Lévi's image of Baphomet was misappropriated in it. The affair caused a scandal throughout the press.

The Société de géographie's hall still exists, and the society has its headquarters there. The facade on boulevard Saint-Germain bears the institution's name. You view it from outside, thinking of that evening when the credulity of an entire era was laid bare. The society still holds public lectures there, as in the 19th century, and the building still houses its library and collections. The boulevard is very busy.

Rue des Beaux-Arts, opened at the beginning of the 19th century, leads into rue de Seine, a stone's throw from the École des beaux-arts and the Institut. It is a neighborhood of booksellers, print dealers and modest hotels; Oscar Wilde would die in 1900 in the hotel on rue des Beaux-Arts. Joséphin Péladan, who had come from Lyon, led the life of a still little-known writer here. His first novels, illustrated by Félicien Rops, were then beginning to make his name in literary circles.

Churton notes that he lived with Henriette Maillat at the top of a house on the corner of the two streets. She, the author of a few novels, had had an affair with Huysmans in 1888; her letters are said to have inspired the character of Mme Chantelouve in Là-bas, a novel about contemporary Satanism. The episode shows how closely the circles of Péladan and Huysmans overlapped before the Boullan affair. Péladan, for his part, was then developing his theories of Idealist art in journals such as L'Artiste.

The book gives neither the number nor the exact dates of the stay. The intersection therefore lends itself to evocation rather than a precise visit: you pass it on the way from Saint-Germain-des-Prés to the Seine. You can see the old facades of these narrow streets, little changed since the 19th century, and then continue to the quai Malaquais and the bouquinistes. The area around the Institut is still one of galleries and booksellers, as it was when Péladan was writing his first books here.

Saint-Sulpice is the largest church on the Left Bank, built between the 17th and 18th centuries. Its first chapel on the right of the entrance, known as the Chapel of the Holy Angels, was decorated by Eugène Delacroix between 1849 and 1861: Jacob Wrestling with the Angel, Heliodorus Driven from the Temple and Saint Michael Vanquishing the Demon. They are among the painter's last major works. The painter worked on them until the end of his life. He painted directly onto the walls.

Churton cites these paintings twice. They fascinated Maurice Barrès, who devoted pages to them that were published after his death, and Péladan saw Delacroix, along with Balzac and Wagner, as one of the intercessors of his aesthetic order. The neighboring seminary is also where Abbé Alphonse-Louis Constant, the future Éliphas Lévi, trained before renouncing the priesthood, which makes Saint-Sulpice a place linked to the origins of French occultism. Lévi had been ordained a deacon there.

The church and the chapel are open to visitors, and the paintings were restored in the early 2010s. Saint-Sulpice's recent fame in mystery novels should not obscure the fact that Churton's book is interested in it for Delacroix and not for any hidden secret. The chapel is immediately on the right as you enter through the main portal, and lighting allows you to see the paintings in detail.

The Café Voltaire occupied the ground floor of a building on place de l'Odéon, opposite the theater. Frequented since the Romantic era, it is mentioned by Balzac. At the end of the 19th century it became a meeting place for Symbolist poets and critics, close to the Latin Quarter and the literary journals of the Left Bank. The café's setting also attracted actors and students. People also came to read the newspapers.

Churton places Gauguin here, back in Paris after Brittany and his stay with Van Gogh in Arles, talking with Aurier, Morice, Redon, Carrière, Moréas and Mirbeau, before leaving for Tahiti in 1891. The Odéon quarter is also where Maurice Barrès introduced Victor-Émile Michelet to Stanislas de Guaita, in the early 1880s; the two young poets were on first-name terms within an hour, according to Michelet. The book does not say which café. Gauguin left for Tahiti in the spring of 1891.

The Café Voltaire closed in the mid-20th century; the publisher Flammarion bought the premises in 1956, and a Histoire de Paris panel now recalls its past. Churton publishes a photograph of its facade. Place de l'Odéon, with its theater, has on the other hand kept the look it had at the end of the 19th century. The square is a convenient starting point for walking to Saint-Sulpice or the Luxembourg Gardens.

Rue Thouin is a small street on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, between rue de l'Estrapade and rue du Cardinal-Lemoine, a few steps from the Panthéon. In the 19th century the neighborhood was home to students, priests and impoverished scholars. Abbé Lacuria (1806-1890), a priest from Lyon who had come to Paris as a tutor, rented a garret here in 1865, after living on rue de Fourcy in the Marais. The rent was modest and the learned libraries close at hand.

In 1844 Lacuria had published Les Harmonies de l'être exprimées par les nombres, a work of Pythagorean theology that caused him difficulties with his superiors. Churton takes up the description by the photographer Félix Thiollier, his former pupil: a nearly silent piano, books everywhere, a wire grill for toasting bread. Péladan, who considered him one of the greatest Platonic theologians, described his visit with emotion. His visitors left marked by his kindness.

Lacuria ended his life in the Lyon region and died blind in Oullins in 1890. The building on rue Thouin is an ordinary residence. The place illustrates the other face of occult Paris: not the fashionable salons, but the discreet transmission of mystical knowledge from an old priest to young admirers. The street remains peaceful and close to place de la Contrescarpe. The Panthéon and rue de l'Estrapade, which Péladan passed along on his visits, are only a few minutes away.

Avenue du Maine, a former country road annexed to Paris in 1860, leads south from the Montparnasse district. Alphonse-Louis Constant (1810-1875), a former seminarian who, under the name Éliphas Lévi, became the leading thinker of French occultism, lived here in the early 1860s. He then made his living from private lessons and from his books, including Dogme et rituel de la haute magie. He also gave consultations to disciples from all over Europe.

Churton reports that an English visitor, Kenneth Mackenzie, came to see him at home on 3 December 1861. Lévi is said to have shown him a prophecy attributed to Paracelsus, read as foretelling the rise of Napoleon, the end of the papacy's political power, Italian unity and the future triumph of the occult sciences. The account, published in 1873, helped spread Lévi's image among English Rosicrucians and later in the Golden Dawn. The episode shows how far Lévi's reputation already reached beyond France's borders.

Lévi died in Paris in 1875; his remains, first buried in Ivry, were later moved to a common grave. The address on avenue du Maine remains one of the few Parisian homes of Lévi precisely documented by Churton. Crowley, who claimed to be his reincarnation, contributed to his posthumous fame. Mackenzie and other foreign visitors thus made this modest dwelling a place of pilgrimage for the first English Rosicrucians. The nearby Gare Montparnasse profoundly transformed the neighborhood in the 20th century.

Paul Ranson (1861-1909) and his wife France moved to 25, boulevard du Montparnasse in 1889. The studio quickly became the weekly meeting place of the Nabis, a group of young painters from the Académie Julian who called themselves “prophets” in Hebrew. They called it the “Temple”, and Ranson acted as host and master of ceremonies. The studio was decorated by the painters themselves. Esoteric texts were also read there.

Churton recalls that on Saturdays they discussed the ideas of Sérusier, back from Brittany where he had painted under Gauguin's guidance, and that Maurice Denis drew from them his famous 1890 text on painting as a flat surface covered with colors. The Nabis were interested in theosophy, in Schuré's Les Grands Initiés and in religious symbolism; several gave themselves nicknames and wore brotherhood garb. Ranson, himself passionate about occultism, painted witches and symbolic scenes.

Ranson later founded the academy that bears his name. The building on boulevard du Montparnasse is private; Churton publishes a photograph of it. The place shows how esoteric ideas also circulated among avant-garde painters, outside occultist circles proper. Several Nabis later exhibited at the Salon de la Rose+Croix, and exchanges between these circles were frequent. In the 20th century Montparnasse would become the great center of artistic life in Paris.

h: Avenue Duquesne is a broad Haussmann-era avenue in the 7th arrondissement, linking place Vauban, behind the dome of the Invalides, to the École militaire. It is a quiet, bourgeois neighborhood, far from Montmartre. The Mathers couple, heads of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, settled in Paris in the early 1890s, first on rue de Miromesnil, then at number 1 on the avenue. The neighborhood offered reasonable rents and respectability, away from bohemian circles.

Churton explains that Mathers presented his order as the heir of the 17th-century English Rosicrucians, which appealed to French Martinist circles. It was in the apartment on avenue Duquesne that the first meetings of the Paris temple were held, named Ahathoor after the Egyptian goddess Hathor. Its official consecration took place on the morning of Saturday 6 January 1894, the feast of the Epiphany, with Mathers as Imperator. Annie Horniman, the order's patron, and William Wynn Westcott, one of its three founders, attended the ceremony.

The temple followed the Mathers to Auteuil the following year. The building on avenue Duquesne is a private residence, and nothing marks this episode. Yet it marks the arrival in Paris of the British magical order that Aleister Crowley would soon join. The first Parisian members were mostly Britons living in France, gradually joined by a few French people. Mathers was also preparing his translations of old grimoires here, such as The Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage.

Auteuil, annexed to Paris in 1860, was still a district of villas and gardens at the end of the 19th century. In 1895 the Mathers rented a house there that could be reached from three streets: avenue Mozart, rue Ribera and rue de la Source. According to Churton, each entrance served a separate part: the garden, the temple and the living quarters. Such a house made it possible to keep family life apart from ritual meetings.

The temple room, adorned with large paintings of Egyptian gods made in Moina's spirit, now housed the Ahathoor temple. Papus was admitted as a neophyte on 23 March 1895, in a ceremony held in French. The astrologer Ely Star, initiated in 1896, became its hierophant in 1899. Churton notes that those close to the Librairie du Merveilleux kept their distance, and that Michelet does not mention it. Rituals were conducted in English or French.

It was here that Aleister Crowley visited Mathers in January 1900, at the time of the crisis pitting the head of the order against its London members. The fate of the villa could not be verified; today the address is simply a landmark in a residential area of the 16th arrondissement. The area, served by the metro, remains residential and peaceful. Rue Ribera and rue de la Source let you walk around the site, and the Maison de Radio France and the Seine are not far away.

Avenue de Wagram, running northeast from the Étoile, was lined with private mansions at the end of the 19th century. Maria de Mariategui, widow of the Count of Medina Pomar and then of the 14th Earl of Caithness, owned a vast house at number 124 that she named Holyrood. Convinced of a spiritual bond with Mary Stuart, she had part of the Scottish palace reproduced and devoted a room to the queen. The richly furnished house included reception rooms, a library and an oratory.

President of a Parisian theosophical society, she received on Wednesdays Guaita, Papus, Oswald Wirth, Albert Jounet, Annie Besant, Jules Bois and Emma Calvé, Charles Richet, Camille Flammarion and the Abbé Roca. It was in this setting, according to Churton, that Jules Doinel's Gnostic Church was consecrated in 1890; the duchess, later elected bishop of Warsaw of this Church, nevertheless declined the office. The book describes, following Doinel, a session in the oratory dedicated to Mary Stuart, lit by a perfumed lamp. All these names recur throughout the book.

Lady Caithness died in 1895, and her death deprived Papus's circle of valuable support. The mansion has since been demolished and replaced by a modern building. You can only walk past the address and imagine the séances held in honor of a Scottish queen beheaded three centuries earlier. Churton's book remains one of the liveliest sources on this salon. His descriptions draw on the accounts of Doinel and Michelet.

h: The Cimetière des Batignolles, opened in 1833 in the northwest of Paris, is now squeezed between the boulevard périphérique and the Épinettes district. Less visited than Père-Lachaise or Montmartre, it nevertheless holds many graves of writers and artists, including Verlaine, André Breton and Édouard Vuillard. It takes its name from the former commune of Batignolles, annexed to Paris in 1860. The entrance is on rue Saint-Just, and a posted map helps you find your way between the divisions.

Joséphin Péladan (1858-1918), born in Lyon, had proclaimed himself “Sâr”, a title of Assyrian origin, and sought to restore an Idealist and Catholic art through his novels, his plays and his Salons. After the Salons ended in 1897, he went on writing, separated from his first wife and lived more quietly. Churton notes that he died at 60 in Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1918, after eating spoiled food. He left a large body of work.

Churton publishes a photograph of his grave among the book's plates. The 6th division is indicated by the cemetery's lists of burials; it is advisable to ask for the map at the entrance. The place offers a sober counterpoint to the splendor of the Salons de la Rose+Croix. It is advisable to check opening hours before visiting. The grave is modest compared with the man's theatrical reputation. The cemetery is quiet.

h: Père-Lachaise, opened in 1804 on the hill of Charonne, is the largest cemetery within the city of Paris. Its 93rd division, in the eastern part near avenue Gambetta, holds the Encausse family grave. Papus was buried there in 1916, later joined by his son Philippe Encausse, also a physician and continuer of the Martinist Order. The cemetery is also the resting place of Allan Kardec, founder of Spiritism, in the 44th division. A map is posted at the entrances.

Papus (1865-1916) was the tireless organizer of French occultism: founder of L'Initiation, of the Martinist Order and of a “group for esoteric studies”, author of treatises on Kabbalah, tarot and magic, he was also a bishop of the Gnostic Church and a traveler to Russia. Churton follows his path up to the war, during which he served as a doctor before dying of tuberculosis. He was also linked to fringe Masonic orders and Russian circles.

The grave bears an inscription of his titles: physician, philosopher, writer, Grand Master of the Martinist Order. It remains a place of passage for those curious about the history of esotericism, and a logical stop for anyone following the traces of occult Paris to its end. Churton publishes a photograph of it among the book's plates. Opening hours vary with the season. It is advisable to check the hours before going, and to bring a map, as the 93rd division is far from the main entrance on boulevard de Ménilmontant.

tl: Rodolphe Salis opens the Chat Noir cabaret on boulevard de Rochechouart; it moves to rue de Laval (now Victor-Massé) in 1885.
Stanislas de Guaita settles on avenue Trudaine; Erik Satie becomes pianist at the Chat Noir at the end of the year.
Guaita and Péladan found the Kabbalistic Order of the Rose-Croix; Papus launches the journal L'Initiation in October.
Opening of Edmond Bailly's Librairie de l'Art indépendant on rue de la Chaussée-d'Antin and of Chamuel's Librairie du Merveilleux on rue de Trévise.
Édouard Schuré publishes Les Grands Initiés; Paul Ranson opens his studio, the Nabis' “Temple”.
Jules Doinel founds the Gnostic Church, consecrated in Lady Caithness's circle; Satie moves to rue Cortot.
Péladan breaks with Guaita and creates the Order of the Catholic Rose+Croix; Huysmans publishes Là-bas.
10 March: after a mass at Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, the first Salon de la Rose+Croix opens at Durand-Ruel's.
Death of Abbé Boullan in Lyon and controversy over “bewitchment”; Satie creates his Metropolitan Church of Art.
6 January: consecration in Paris of the Golden Dawn's Ahathoor Temple No. 7, at the Mathers' home.
Papus is received into the Golden Dawn in Auteuil; death of Lady Caithness in November.
Fifth Salon de la Rose+Croix at the Galerie des Arts réunis, with a poster that causes a scandal.
Last Salon de la Rose+Croix at Georges Petit's; Léo Taxil confesses his hoax; death of Guaita in December.
Satie leaves Montmartre for Arcueil; deaths of Gustave Moreau and Mallarmé.
The Mathers present their Rites of Isis at the Théâtre de la Bodinière.
Aleister Crowley visits Mathers in Auteuil, in the midst of the Golden Dawn crisis.
The Gustave Moreau museum on rue de La Rochefoucauld opens to the public.
Theodor Reuss grants Papus a charter for the rites of Memphis and Misraïm.
Death of Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, theorist of synarchy.
